﴿Indeed, We have granted you a clear victory﴾ ﴿that Allah may forgive you your sins, past and future, complete His favor upon you, and guide you to a straight path﴾ ﴿and that Allah may help you with a mighty help﴾ ﴿It is He who sent down tranquility into the hearts of the believers that they might increase in faith along with their faith—and to Allah belong the soldiers of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾

Some people said—as al-Zahrawi related—: ﴿We have granted you﴾ means the conquest of Makkah. al-Tha'labi also related this, and al-Naqqash attributed it to al-Kalbi. He (Allah) informed of it in the sense of: We decreed it. And "al-Fattah" in the dialect of Yemen means the judge. It was also said: the meaning is, "Indeed We have opened for you" by guiding you to Islam, "that He may forgive." The majority of people—and the correct view, which the story of al-Hudaybiyya supports—said: the meaning of His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Indeed, We have granted you﴾ is only: what Allah facilitated for you in that expedition is a clear victory that you will encounter. The surah was revealed to comfort the believers, because they had been distressed by Quraysh's turning them back and by that truce which the Prophet ﷺ had concluded with them. So the surah came to console them regarding their being barred from the House, and to remove what was in their hearts. From this is the famous hadith of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), and what he said to the Prophet ﷺ and to Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him). The Messenger of Allah ﷺ, on that journey, anticipated that he had made a truce with his enemy until he himself would grow strong. There appeared at his hands the sign of water in the well of al-Hudaybiyya, when he placed his arrow in it and the water gushed forth until it sufficed the army. The Pledge of al-Ridwan took place, and it was the greatest conquest, as said by Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah and al-Bara' ibn 'Azib. And his offering reached its place, as said by al-Sha'bi. And he anticipated the conquest of Khaybar, and the hands of the believers were filled with good; and it was conquered only by the people of al-Hudaybiyya, and no one shared it with them. But this requires examination, because the people of the ship with Ja'far ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) shared with them in the distribution. Therefore it should be said: no one among those who had stayed behind from al-Hudaybiyya shared with them. In that same period there occurred a great battle between the Romans and the Persians in which the Romans prevailed, and this was part of the conquest for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; he and the believers were delighted by it, because the People of the Book prevailed over the Magians and the greatest power of disbelief was broken.

Then Allah, may He be exalted, magnified the matter of His Prophet ﷺ and honored him by informing him that He had forgiven him his past and future sins. His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿"that He may forgive"﴾ is the lam of "kay" (purpose), but it differs from it in meaning. The intended meaning here is that Allah granted you victory so that He might make that a sign and token of His forgiveness of you. So it is like the lam of ṣayrūra (resulting consequence). For this reason the peace and blessings of Allah be upon him said: "Tonight there was sent down to me a surah that is dearer to me (p-666) than the world." al-Tabari and Ibn Kaysan said: the meaning is: "Indeed We have granted you victory, so glorify your Lord with His praise and seek His forgiveness, that He may forgive you," and they connected this verse with His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿When the help of Allah and the victory comes﴾ [al-Nasr: 1]. This is weak in two respects. First, the surah ﴿When the help of Allah comes﴾ [al-Nasr: 1] was revealed at the very end of the Prophet's ﷺ life, announcing his own death, as Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said when he asked 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) about it. Second, the honoring of the Prophet ﷺ by singling him out would vanish, because every believer is addressed by what al-Tabari said, namely: "Glorify and seek forgiveness so that Allah may forgive you." This does not imply that the forgiveness has already occurred, whereas what we mentioned first implies that forgiveness has occurred for the Prophet ﷺ. This is shown by the statement of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) to him ﷺ when he stood (in prayer) until his feet swelled: "Do you do this, O Messenger of Allah, when Allah has forgiven you your past and future sins?" He said: "Should I not be a grateful servant?" This is a clear text that forgiveness has indeed occurred. Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: the meaning is: your striving for the sake of Allah, the Most High, coupled with the victory, is for the purpose of forgiveness. al-Tha'labi related from al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl that the meaning is: "Indeed We have granted you victory, so seek forgiveness for your sin and for the believing men and women, that Allah may forgive you..." the verse; and this is similar to al-Tabari's view.

As for His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿what is past of your sin and what is to come﴾, Sufyan al-Thawri said: "what is past" refers to (p-667) the period before prophethood, and "what is to come" is everything he did not know. This is weak. The real meaning is honoring through this ruling, even if he had no sins at all. The scholars unanimously agreed on the infallibility of the Prophets, peace be upon them, from major sins and from minor sins that are base vices. [Some of them permitted minor sins that are not base vices.] They differed as to whether such a thing occurred from Muhammad ﷺ or not. al-Tha'labi related from 'Ata' al-Khurasani that he said: "what is past" is the sin of Adam and Eve, peace be upon them, that is, by your blessing; and "what is to come" is the sins of your community, through your supplication. al-Tha'labi said: the Imamiyya do not permit minor sins for the Prophet ﷺ or for the Imam, and the verse refutes them. Some of them said: "what is past" is his peace and blessings be upon him saying on the day of Badr: "O Allah, if this band perishes, You will not be worshipped," and "what is to come" is his peace and blessings be upon him saying on the day of Hunayn: "We will not be overcome today for lack of numbers." All of this is objectionable.

The "completion of His favor upon him" is his manifestation and his prevailing over his enemy, and the good pleasure (of Allah) in the Hereafter. His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿and guide you to a straight path﴾ means: to a straight path; the preposition is omitted so the verb becomes transitive, and this verb may be transitive without a preposition. "A mighty help" is that in which there is the overpowering of the enemy and prevailing over him; help that is not mighty is that whose content is only protection and repelling the enemy. "The sending down of tranquility into the hearts of the believers"—and it is a noun of action from "sukūn" (stillness)—is its calming with respect to that truce with Quraysh until they were reassured and knew that Allah's promise through His Messenger ﷺ is true, so they increased in faith beyond their first faith and their affirmation grew. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: when they believed in tawhid, the acts of worship increased them little by little, so they kept increasing in faith until He said to them: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], and He granted them the most perfect faith of the people of the heavens and the earth: "There is no god but Allah." Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) interpreted "tranquility" as mercy. His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿and to Allah belong the soldiers of the heavens and the earth﴾ is an indication of the calming of souls too, and that they should be submissive, because He helps whenever He wills and in whatever form He wills, in ways that human beings cannot plan; and among His soldiers is the tranquility which He sent down into the hearts of the Companions of Muhammad ﷺ, thus steadying their insight. His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿and Allah is﴾ means: and He is/will be; it indicates existence with this attribute, not restricted to a past time. "Knowledge" and "wisdom" are two attributes that necessitate the might of victory for whomever the one described by them wills to help.

[p. 668]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That He may admit the believing men and believing women into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein eternally, and remove from them their misdeeds; and that is with Allah a great achievement.﴾ ﴿And that He may punish the hypocrite men and hypocrite women, and the polytheist men and polytheist women, who assume about Allah an assumption of evil. Upon them is the turn of evil. Allah has become angry with them, and has cursed them, and has prepared for them Hell, and it is an evil destination.﴾ ﴿To Allah belong the soldiers of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is ever Mighty and Wise.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That they may increase in faith along with their faith﴾ [48:4] means: so they increased and received that. Then, after that, His saying, ﴿That He may admit the believing men﴾, meaning: by their acquiring acceptance of what Allah the Exalted sent down to them. It is also related concerning the meaning of this verse that when ﴿And I do not know what will be done with me or with you﴾ [46:9] was revealed, the People of the Book (Jews and Christians) spoke about it and said: "How can we follow one who does not know what will be done with him and with the people who are with him?" So Allah clarified in this surah what will be done with him, by His saying, ﴿that Allah may forgive you your past and future sins﴾ [48:2]. When the believers heard it, they said: "Hani'an mari'an (may it be pleasant and wholesome), O Messenger of Allah, this is for you. So what is for us?" Then this verse was revealed: ﴿That He may admit the believing men and believing women into gardens﴾, up to His saying: ﴿and it is an evil destination﴾. Thus Allah informed him of what will be done with him, and with the believers and the disbelievers. Al-Naqqash mentioned that a man from 'Akk said: "This is for you, O Messenger of Allah, so what is for us?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It is for me and for my community like these two," and he joined his two fingers.

His saying, ﴿And that He may remove from them their misdeeds﴾, contains an ordering of the clauses in the narrative, not an ordering of the occurrence of their meanings; for the expiation of misdeeds precedes their admission into Paradise.

[p. 669] His saying, ﴿who assume about Allah an assumption of evil﴾: it was said that its meaning derives from their saying: ﴿the Messenger and the believers will never return to their families﴾ [48:12], and so on. It is as if they assumed an evil assumption about Allah concerning the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers. It was also said: they assumed an evil assumption about Allah the Exalted, since they believed in Him without His attributes. So these are evil assumptions in that they are false, leading to their punishment in the Fire of Hell.

His saying, ﴿Upon them is the turn of evil﴾, seems to strengthen the other interpretation, meaning: what they intended for you has befallen them. The majority of readers recited: "'alayhim da'iratu l-sau'" as the first, and al-Farra' preferred it, saying: "The Arabs rarely pronounce the sin with a damma." Abu 'Ali said: "They are close in meaning, and the fatha is more consistent with the wording." Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited: "zanna l-sau'" with a fatha on the sin, and "'alayhim da'iratu l-sau'" with a damma on the sin, which is a noun, meaning: the turn of evil that they intended for you in their evil assumption. Al-Hasan recited with a damma on the sin in both places, and this is related from Abu 'Amr and Mujahid.

Allah the Exalted named the calamity by which He invoked against them a "turn" (da'ira), from the fact that it is said of time that it revolves. Do you not see that the year and the month are as if they revolve, going in order and coming from where they are measures of the great motion? From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed time has turned back to its form on the day Allah created the heavens and the earth." So the decrees and events that are within the folds of time are called a "turn", because they turn with the turning of time. It is as if you say: such a matter will happen on such a day of such a year. Because that day turns until it emerges into existence, the matter also turns within it.

[p. 670] From this is the saying of the poet:

"And the vicissitudes of time have indeed turned."

From it is also the saying of another:

"And he knows that calamities turn."

This is abundant. It is fitting to call a calamity a "turn" because of its completeness, that it encircles its owner just as the shape of a circle encircles, equally, from the point. Al-Naqqash has indicated this meaning.

As for "Allah became angry" (ghadiba Allahu): when it is intended as will, it is an attribute of essence (sifat dhat); when it is intended as what appears of actions upon the one who is angered, it is an attribute of action (sifat fi'l). So each expression has an aspect of meaning. Ibn al-Mubarak said in the book of al-Naqqash: the soldiers of Allah in the heavens are the angels, and on earth are the warriors in the way of Allah the Exalted.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"This is a part of a whole."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 48, verses 8–10:

The words of the Exalted:

﴿Indeed, We have sent you as a witness, a bringer of good news, and a warner.﴾ ﴿So that you (people) may believe in Allah and His Messenger, support him, honour him, and glorify Him morning and evening.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you are only pledging allegiance to Allah. The hand of Allah is above their hands. So whoever breaks his pledge, breaks it only to his own harm, and whoever fulfils what he has covenanted with Allah, He will give him a great reward.﴾

(p-671) Whoever takes "witness" (al-shahid) to mean the one who obtains the testimony (muhassil al-shahada), from the day he obtains it, then His saying, ﴿shahidan﴾ ("as a witness"), is a present circumstantial clause (hal waqi'a). Whoever takes "witness" to mean the one who delivers the testimony (mu'addi al-shahada), then it is a future circumstantial clause (hal mustaqbila), which the grammarians call the "anticipated" (al-muqaddara). The meaning is: a witness over people for their deeds and their words, from the time the Law reached them; a bringer of good news to the people of obedience of the mercy of Allah, the Exalted; and a warner to the people of disbelief, warning them of the punishment of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Most reciters in all the regions read ﴿لِتُؤْمِنُوا﴾ ("so that you may believe") with the second person, addressing the people, meaning: say to them. The three verbs that follow are likewise. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala', Ibn Kathir and Abu Ja'far read ﴿لِيُؤْمِنُوا﴾ ("so that they may believe") with the yā' (third person), continuing the address to Muhammad (ﷺ), and the three verbs that follow are likewise. Al-Jahdari read ﴿وَتُعَزِّرُوهُ﴾ with a fatha on the tā', a sukun on the 'ayn and a damma on the zā'. Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' al-Yamani and Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) read ﴿وَتُعَزِّزُوهُ﴾ with two zā's, from al-'izza (might). Ja'far ibn Muhammad read ﴿وَتُعَزِّرُوهُ﴾ with a fatha on the tā', a sukun on the 'ayn and a kasra on the zā'. The meaning of ﴿تُعَزِّرُوهُ﴾ is: you glorify him and magnify him; this is what Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said. Qatada said: its meaning is: you support him with fighting. Some of the interpreters said: the pronouns in His saying, ﴿وَتُعَزِّرُوهُ وَتُوَقِّرُوهُ وَتُسَبِّحُوهُ﴾, all refer to Allah, the Exalted. Most scholars said: ﴿تُعَزِّرُوهُ وَتُوَقِّرُوهُ﴾ both refer to the Prophet (ﷺ), and ﴿تُسَبِّحُوهُ﴾ refers to Allah, the Exalted, and this is the prayer of the two cool times (salat al-bardayn). 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) read ﴿وَتُسَبِّحُوا اللهَ﴾. In some of what Abu Hatim transmitted it is ﴿وَتُسَبِّحُونَ اللهَ﴾ with the nun. ﴿The bedouins who were left behind will say to you: "Our possessions and our families occupied us, so ask forgiveness for us." They say with their tongues what is not in their hearts. (p-676) The Almighty said:

﴿Say to the Bedouins who were left behind: "You will be called to face a people of great might; you will fight them, or they will submit. So if you obey, Allah will give you a good reward, but if you turn away as you turned away before, He will punish you with a painful punishment."﴾

Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet ﷺ to forewarn these left-behind ones that they would be summoned to fight a formidable enemy. This indicates that they used to show Islam, for otherwise they would not have been fit for that (the latter matter).

The people differed concerning the folk referred to in His words ﴿a people of great might﴾. 'Ikrimah, Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah said: they are Hawazin and those who fought the Messenger of Allah ﷺ at Hunayn. Included in this view, in my opinion, are those who were fought and defeated at the Conquest of Makkah. Ka'b said: they are the Romans, whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out against in the year of Tabuk, and those to whom he sent (an army) at the battle of Mu'tah. Al-Zuhri and al-Kalbi said: they are the people of apostasy (ahl al-Riddah) and Banu Hanifah in al-Yamamah. Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: it follows from this view that the verse indicates the caliphate of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with them both, meaning: when the unseen was disclosed, that they both called to fight the people of apostasy. Al-Tha'labi related from Rafi' ibn Khadij that he said: "By Allah, we used to recite this verse in the past and did not know who they were, until Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, called to fight Banu Hanifah, and then we knew that they were them." Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Abi Layla said: they are the Persians. Al-Hasan said: they are Persia and the Romans. Abu Hurayrah said: they are a people who have not yet come. Mundhir ibn Sa'id also said: Allah lifted the jizyah in this (case), and there is only fighting or Islam, and this is found only among the people of apostasy.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

And it is the one who was fought at the Conquest of Makkah.

The majority read ﴿"or they will submit"﴾ in the indicative (al-qat'), meaning: or they will submit without war. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, as transmitted by al-Kisa'i, read "or they submit" (aslamu) with the verb in the subjunctive, on the assumption: "or it will be that they submit" (aw yakuna an yuslimu). A similar example from poetry is the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

Then I said to her: "Do not weep, your eyes, for we are only seeking a kingdom, or we die and are excused."

It is related as "namuta" with both the subjunctive and the indicative. The subjunctive is on the assumption: "or it will be that we die," and the indicative is on the basis of the independent clause (al-qat'): "or we are dying."

His words ﴿So if you obey﴾ mean: in what you are called to. The punishment with which He threatened them may be understood to refer to the punishment of this world; as for the punishment of the Hereafter, it is clear in regard to them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 48, verse 17–19:

And the saying of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor is there blame upon the lame, nor is there blame upon the sick. And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger – He will admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow; and whoever turns away – He will punish him with a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿Allah was certainly pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree, and He knew what was in their hearts, so He sent down tranquillity upon them and rewarded them with a near victory.﴾ ﴿And much booty that they will take. And Allah is ever Exalted in Might and Wise.﴾

When the Mighty and Majestic reached, in rebuking those who stayed behind from the tribes adjacent to Madinah, "such as Juhaynah, Muzaynah, Ghifar, Aslam and Ashja'," He followed that by excusing the people of excuses – the blind, the lame and the sick – collectively, and lifting from them the hardship, the constraint and the sin. This is the ruling for these excused persons in every jihad until the Day of Resurrection, except that when a party is confronted in some presence, the obligation falls according to capacity. Along with the removal of hardship, it is permissible for them to go on raids, and their reward for it is multiplied, because the lame man is the most deserving of people of patience and of not fleeing. Ibn Umm Maktum went on a raid and was holding the banner during some of the battles of (p-678) al-Qadisiyyah. Al-Nasa'i transmitted this meaning and mentioned Ibn Umm Maktum, may Allah be pleased with him.

The majority of reciters read "yudkhiluhu" with the ya', while Ibn 'Amir, Nafi', Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj, al-Hasan, Shaybah and Qatadah read "nudkhiluhu" with the nun. Likewise "yu'adhdhibuhu" and "nu'adhdhibuhu."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah was certainly pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree﴾ is an honouring and an announcement of His pleasure with them at the time of the pledge, and for this reason it was named the Pledge of Ridwan. Al-Ridha (pleasure) here means the will, so it is an attribute of essence. As for one who takes "idh" as causal, meaning: "because they pledged allegiance under the tree," it is permissible to take "radiya" to mean: the manifestation of blessings upon them, on account of their pledge, so al-ridha, on this reading, is an attribute of action. The discussion of the pledge (mubaya'ah) and its meaning has already preceded.

The cause of this pledge was that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ wished to send to Makkah a man to make clear to the Quraysh that the Prophet ﷺ did not desire war, and that he had only come as a pilgrim performing 'umrah. So he sent to them Khirash ibn Umayyah al-Khuza'i, and mounted him on a camel called al-Tha'lab. When he spoke to them, they hamstrung the camel and wished to kill Khirash, but the Ahabish prevented him. This reached the Prophet ﷺ, and he wished to send 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him. 'Umar said: "O Messenger of Allah, you know my harshness towards the Quraysh, and they hate me, and there is no one from the Banu 'Adi ibn Ka'b to protect me; but send 'Uthman ibn 'Affan." So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent him, and he went. Aban ibn Sa'id ibn al-'As met him, dismounted from his mount, carried him upon it, and gave him protection, until he reached the Quraysh and informed them. They said to him: "If you wish, O 'Uthman, to circumambulate the House, then circumambulate it; but as for your entering upon us, there is no way to that." 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I would not circumambulate it until the Messenger of Allah ﷺ circumambulates it." Then the sons of Sa'id ibn al-'As detained 'Uthman by way of kindness, and he was late in returning to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Al-Hudaybiyah was ten miles from Makkah. A cry was raised from the army of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "'Uthman has been killed!" So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the believers became incensed and said: "We will not depart if this is so until we meet the people." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ called to the pledge, and his caller proclaimed: "O people, the pledge! The pledge!" The Spirit of Holiness descended, and none of those who witnessed al-Hudaybiyah lagged behind the pledge except al-Jadd ibn Qays the hypocrite. At that time the Messenger of Allah ﷺ placed his hand upon his own hand and said: "This is the hand of 'Uthman, and it is better than the hand of 'Uthman." Then 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, came back safely after that.

The tree was a samurah (acacia-type tree) that was there; it disappeared after years. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, passed by the site during his caliphate, and his companions disagreed about its location. 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Proceed; this is over-exertion."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and He knew what was in their hearts﴾. Some people said: its meaning is: [what was in their hearts] of dislike for pledging on death and the like; but this is weak, as it contains a reproach to the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. Al-Tabari and Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: its meaning is: [what was in their hearts] of faith, its soundness, love for the religion, and eagerness for it. This is a good saying, but whoever has this state does not need the descent of that which calms him, except that it is possible he is rewarded with tranquillity, the near victory, and the booty. Others said: its meaning is: [what was in their hearts] of the concern to turn away from the polytheists and the resentment at that, in the manner in which 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and others addressed it. This is a good interpretation, with which the descent of tranquillity and the allusion to the near victory are consistent. Tranquillity here means the settling of their hearts and their being made submissive to accept the command of Allah, exalted is He, and to be patient for Him. The people read: ﴿"wa-athabahum"﴾. Harun said: it has also been read "wa-atabahum" with a ta' with two dots above.

"The near victory" is Khaybar, because the Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned with the believers to Madinah, and Allah had promised him Khaybar, and he set out toward it without delay. Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: it has also been said: the near victory is the conquest of Makkah, and "the abundant booty" is the conquest of Khaybar. Ya'qub, in the transmission of Ruways, read "ta'khudhunaha" with the ta' from above, addressing them directly; the majority read ﴿"ya'khudhunaha"﴾ in the third person.

There was disagreement about the number of those who pledged. It was said: one thousand five hundred, related by Qatadah; it was said: and four hundred, related by Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah; it was said: and five hundred and twenty-five, related by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both; it was said: and three hundred, related by Ibn Abi Awfa; and other figures have been said beyond what we have mentioned before. The first to pledge in that was a man from the Banu Asad called Abu Sinan ibn Wahb, related by al-Sha'bi.

And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger – He will admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow; and whoever turns away – He will punish him with a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿Allah was certainly pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree, and He knew what was in their hearts, so He sent down tranquillity upon them and rewarded them with a near victory.﴾ ﴿And much booty that they will take. And Allah is ever Exalted in Might and Wise.﴾

When the Mighty and Majestic reached, in rebuking those who stayed behind from the tribes adjacent to Madinah, "such as Juhaynah, Muzaynah, Ghifar, Aslam and Ashja'," He followed that by excusing the people of excuses – the blind, the lame and the sick – collectively, and lifting from them the hardship, the constraint and the sin. This is the ruling for these excused persons in every jihad until the Day of Resurrection, except that when a party is confronted in some presence, the obligation falls according to capacity. Along with the removal of hardship, it is permissible for them to go on raids, and their reward for it is multiplied, because the lame man is the most deserving of people of patience and of not fleeing. Ibn Umm Maktum went on a raid and was holding the banner during some of the battles of (p-678) al-Qadisiyyah. Al-Nasa'i transmitted this meaning and mentioned Ibn Umm Maktum, may Allah be pleased with him.

The majority of reciters read "yudkhiluhu" with the ya', while Ibn 'Amir, Nafi', Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj, al-Hasan, Shaybah and Qatadah read "nudkhiluhu" with the nun. Likewise "yu'adhdhibuhu" and "nu'adhdhibuhu."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah was certainly pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree﴾ is an honouring and an announcement of His pleasure with them at the time of the pledge, and for this reason it was named the Pledge of Ridwan. Al-Ridha (pleasure) here means the will, so it is an attribute of essence. As for one who takes "idh" as causal, meaning: "because they pledged allegiance under the tree," it is permissible to take "radiya" to mean: the manifestation of blessings upon them, on account of their pledge, so al-ridha, on this reading, is an attribute of action. The discussion of the pledge (mubaya'ah) and its meaning has already preceded.

The cause of this pledge was that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ wished to send to Makkah a man to make clear to the Quraysh that the Prophet ﷺ did not desire war, and that he had only come as a pilgrim performing 'umrah. So he sent to them Khirash ibn Umayyah al-Khuza'i, and mounted him on a camel called al-Tha'lab. When he spoke to them, they hamstrung the camel and wished to kill Khirash, but the Ahabish prevented him. This reached the Prophet ﷺ, and he wished to send 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him. 'Umar said: "O Messenger of Allah, you know my harshness towards the Quraysh, and they hate me, and there is no one from the Banu 'Adi ibn Ka'b to protect me; but send 'Uthman ibn 'Affan." So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent him, and he went. Aban ibn Sa'id ibn al-'As met him, dismounted from his mount, carried him upon it, and gave him protection, until he reached the Quraysh and informed them. They said to him: "If you wish, O 'Uthman, to circumambulate the House, then circumambulate it; but as for your entering upon us, there is no way to that." 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I would not circumambulate it until the Messenger of Allah ﷺ circumambulates it." Then the sons of Sa'id ibn al-'As detained 'Uthman by way of kindness, and he was late in returning to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Al-Hudaybiyah was ten miles from Makkah. A cry was raised from the army of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "'Uthman has been killed!" So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the believers became incensed and said: "We will not depart if this is so until we meet the people." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ called to the pledge, and his caller proclaimed: "O people, the pledge! The pledge!" The Spirit of Holiness descended, and none of those who witnessed al-Hudaybiyah lagged behind the pledge except al-Jadd ibn Qays the hypocrite. At that time the Messenger of Allah ﷺ placed his hand upon his own hand and said: "This is the hand of 'Uthman, and it is better than the hand of 'Uthman." Then 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, came back safely after that.

The tree was a samurah (acacia-type tree) that was there; it disappeared after years. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, passed by the site during his caliphate, and his companions disagreed about its location. 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Proceed; this is over-exertion."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and He knew what was in their hearts﴾. Some people said: its meaning is: [what was in their hearts] of dislike for pledging on death and the like; but this is weak, as it contains a reproach to the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. Al-Tabari and Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: its meaning is: [what was in their hearts] of faith, its soundness, love for the religion, and eagerness for it. This is a good saying, but whoever has this state does not need the descent of that which calms him, except that it is possible he is rewarded with tranquillity, the near victory, and the booty. Others said: its meaning is: [what was in their hearts] of the concern to turn away from the polytheists and the resentment at that, in the manner in which 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and others addressed it. There was disagreement about the number of those who pledged. It was said: one thousand five hundred, related by Qatadah; it was said: and four hundred, related by Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah; it was said: and five hundred and twenty-five, related by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both; it was said: and three hundred, related by Ibn Abi Awfa; and other figures have been said beyond what we have mentioned before. The first to pledge in that was a man from the Banu Asad called Abu Sinan ibn Wahb, related by al-Sha'bi.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 48, verses 20–24:

His Exalted and Majestic words:

﴿Allah has promised you much booty that you will take, and He has hastened this for you, and restrained the hands of the people from you, that it may be a sign for the believers and that He may guide you to a straight path.﴾ ﴿And other [gains] you were not able to obtain, but Allah has already encompassed them, and Allah is ever competent over all things.﴾ ﴿And if those who disbelieved had fought you, they would have turned their backs; then they would not have found any ally or helper.﴾ ﴿[This is] the way of Allah which has already occurred before; and you will not find in the way of Allah any change.﴾ ﴿And it is He who restrained their hands from you and your hands from them within [the valley of] Makkah after He had given you victory over them. And ever is Allah, of what you do, Seeing.﴾

His words, "Allah has promised you" (the verse), address the believers, and it is a promise of all the spoils that the Muslims have taken and will take until the Day of Resurrection, as said by Mujahid and others. His words, "and He has hastened this for you," mean Khaybar. Zayd ibn Aslam and his son said: "much booty" is Khaybar, and "this" refers to the Pledge (al-bay'ah) and the deliverance from the affair of the Quraysh. His words, "and restrained the hands of the people from you," mean those who took charge of the vulnerability of Madinah after the Prophet ﷺ and the believers left it. That is because among the Arab tribes and the Jews there were those who were hostile, and they had been given an opportunity, so Allah the Exalted restrained them from the offspring and property of the Muslims. This is a sign for the believers that Allah the Exalted helps them and is gentle with them, as said by Qatadah. Al-Tha'labi related that he said: Allah the Exalted restrained Ghatafan from the Prophet ﷺ when they came to support the people of Khaybar; this was also mentioned by al-Naqqash. Al-Tha'labi also said, from some of them: it meant the restraint of the Quraysh.

His words, "and other [gains] you were not able to obtain," Abdullah ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: it refers to the lands of Persia and Rome. Al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd said: it refers to Khaybar. Qatadah and al-Hasan said: it refers to Makkah, and this is the view with which the meaning is consistent and confirmed. His words, "Allah has already encompassed them," mean: with power and dominance over their people; that is, He had already foreknown this in His knowledge, and it became manifest in them that they would not be able to obtain them.

His words, "And if those who disbelieved had fought you, they would have turned their backs," refer to the Quraysh and those allied with them in that year, as said by Qatadah. In this there is strengthening for the hearts of the believers. Some exegetes said: it means Rome and Persia, but this is weak; rather the reference is to the nearby enemy.

His words, "the way of Allah," refer to the battle of Badr. It was said: it refers to the habit of Allah the Exalted of granting victory to the prophets (peace be upon them) in former times. "Sunnata" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), and the nominative is permissible, though it was not recited with it.

His words, "And it is He who restrained their hands," (the verse), it is related concerning its occasion that "the Quraysh gathered a group of their youths and put them with Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl, and they went out seeking an opening in the army of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. People differed greatly over the number of these, so I have abridged it. When the Muslims sensed them, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent after them Khalid ibn al-Walid, whom he then named 'the Sword of Allah,' with a company of people, they fled before them until they brought them into the houses of Makkah; they captured a number of them, and they were brought to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who showed them favour and released them." This is the meaning of Allah restraining their hands from the Muslims through terror, and restraining the hands of the Muslims from them by prohibiting [them from attacking] within the houses of Makkah and elsewhere; and that is "the valley of Makkah." Qatadah said: the Prophet ﷺ captured this group at al-Hudaybiyah near his army and showed them favour, and that is "the valley of Makkah." Al-Naqqash said: all of the Sacred Precinct is Makkah, and the victory over them is the capture of those among them who were taken. And in this verse there is an exhortation to righteous deeds, for whoever feels that Allah sees his deed will perfect it.

The majority of reciters read "taʿmalūna" (what you do) with the ta' as address (the second person). Abu 'Amr alone read it with the ya', referring to the disbelievers and as a warning to them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 48, verses 25–26:

His, may He be exalted and glorified, saying:

﴿They are the ones who disbelieved, and barred you from the Sacred Mosque, and the offering detained from reaching its place of sacrifice. Had it not been for believing men and believing women whom you did not know, that you might trample them and thereby incur a liability without knowledge — [that God might admit into His mercy whom He wills. Had they been separated, We would have punished those among them who disbelieved with a painful punishment.] ﴾ ﴿When those who disbelieved put into their hearts zealotry — the zealotry of the Jahiliyya — then God sent down His tranquillity upon His Messenger and upon the believers, and imposed on them the word of piety, and they were more deserving of it and worthy of it. And God is ever Knowing of all things.﴾

By His saying ﴿They are the ones who disbelieved﴾, God, may He be exalted, means the people of Makkah who were mentioned earlier. His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿and barred you from the Sacred Mosque﴾ refers to their preventing the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions from performing the 'umrah in the year of al-Hudaybiyya. That was because "the Prophet ﷺ set out from Madinah in Dhu al-Qa'dah of the sixth year after the Hijra, intending the 'umrah and the glorification of the House, and went out with him with one hundred camels (badana)," as related by al-Naqqash; it was also said: seventy, as related by al-Musawwar ibn Makhrama and Marwan ibn al-Hakam. "When he drew near to Makkah, the people of Makkah said: This is Muhammad, who has fought us and killed among us, and he wishes to enter Makkah in defiance of us. By God, we will not leave him until we die defending against that." So they gathered to fight him, sought help from tribes of the Arabs, namely the Ahabish, and they sent and polluted for the Messenger of God ﷺ the waters near Makkah. The Messenger of God ﷺ came until he halted at the well of al-Hudaybiyya, and at that time he placed his arrow in the water, and it flowed abundantly until it sufficed the army. Then the Messenger of God ﷺ sent 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may God be pleased with him, to Makkah, and the people of Makkah sent men to him, among them 'Urwa ibn Mas'ud and Budayl ibn Warqa'. The Messenger of God ﷺ remained there for days until Suhayl ibn 'Amr travelled, and with him the truce was concluded on the condition that the Messenger of God ﷺ would turn back from them and perform the 'umrah in the coming year. This was their barring of him." It is comprehensively recorded in the books of biography, so we have abridged it.

Al-Jumhur read "wal-hadya" (والهَدْيَ) with a sukun on the dal; al-A'raj and al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read "wal-hadiyy" (والهَدِيُّ) with a kasra on the dal and a shadda on the ya; both are dialectal forms. It is coordinated with the pronoun in His saying ﴿and barred you﴾, meaning: and they barred the offering. "Ma'kufan" (مَعْكُوفًا) is a circumstantial accusative (hal), and its meaning is "detained"; one says "'akaftu al-rajul 'an hajatihi" when I detained the man from his need. Abu 'Ali said that "'akafa" is not known to be transitive, while Ibn Sida and others related its transitivity. This detention of the offering came from the polytheists through their barring, and from the Muslims through their seeing and managing its affair, so they detained their offering. The "an" (أنْ) in His saying ﴿that it reach its place of sacrifice﴾ may be governed by the barring, as if He said: "they barred the offering out of dislike that, or from that," and it may be governed by the detention, in which case "an" is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), i.e., the offering detained for the sake of its reaching its place of sacrifice; this is the detention of the Muslims, for the detention of the polytheists was not for the sake of the offering reaching its place. "Mahallahu" (مَحِلَّهُ) means Makkah and the House.

(p-٦٨٣) God, exalted is He, mentioned the reason why the Muslims were turned back and He did not enable them to enter Makkah in that manner: that there were believers in Makkah, men and women, whose faith was hidden; so if the Muslims had overrun its territory they would have destroyed those believers. Qatada said: God thus repelled the polytheists by the blessing of those believers, and He may repel the disbelievers through the believers. His saying ﴿you did not know﴾ is a description of those mentioned. His saying ﴿that you might trample them﴾ may be a substitute (badal) for "rijal" (men), as if He said: "had it not been for a believing people that you might trample them," i.e., had it not been for your trampling a believing people; on this reading it is in the nominative position. It may also be in the accusative position as a substitute for the pronoun in His saying ﴿you did not know them﴾, as if He said: "you did not know their being trampled was the trampling of believers." "Al-wat'" (الوَطْءُ) here means destruction by the sword and other means, in the sense of metaphor; from it is the line of the poet:

"You trod upon us with a treading in rage, / the treading of one shackled, whose hair has grown white."

From it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "O God, tighten Your grip (wat'ataka) upon Mudar." And from it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed the last trampling (wat'a) of the Lord is at the day of Wajj in al-Ta'if," because it was the last encounter of the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Naqqash mentioned this meaning.

(p-٦٨٤) "Al-ma'arra" (المَعَرَّةُ) is evil and an adhering hatefulness, derived from "al-'arr" and "al-'urra", which is a severe, persistent mange. People differed in specifying this ma'arra. Ibn Zayd said: it is sin (ma'tham). Ibn Ishaq said: it is blood-money (diya). These two are weak, because there is neither sin nor blood-money in killing a believer whose faith is concealed among the people of war. Al-Tabari — related by al-Tha'labi — said: it is expiation (kaffara). Mundhir said: al-ma'arra is that the disbelievers would blame them and say: they killed the people of their own religion. Some of the exegetes said: it is blame and speech about that, and the soul's distress over it for the rest of time; these are the sayings of Hassan. The response of "law la" (لَوْلا) is omitted, its estimated meaning being: "We would have enabled you to enter Makkah and given you victory over them." Al-A'mash read: "fatanalakum minhu ma'arratun" (فَتَنالُكم مِنهُ مَعَرَّةٌ).

The lam in His saying ﴿li-yudkhila﴾ (لِيُدْخِلَ) may be connected with an omitted element of speech, its estimated meaning being: "Were it not for these, you would have entered Makkah; but these believers were honoured by Us in that We showed them mercy and repelled through them [the danger] from Makkah, so that God might admit," i.e., so that He might make clear to the observer that God admits whom He wills into His mercy; or, i.e., so that their entry into the mercy of God and His repelling [the harm] from them would take place. It may also be connected to the previously mentioned faith, as if He said: "Had it not been for believing people who believed, so that God might admit into His mercy," and this is mentioned, but it is weak, because His saying ﴿whom He wills﴾ weakens this interpretation.

Then His saying ﴿had they been separated (law tazayyalu)﴾, i.e., had they departed from Makkah. One says "zayyaltu Zaydan 'an mawdi'ihi izalatan," meaning I removed Zayd from his place, i.e., I made him go; this verb is not from "zala yazulu," though it has been said that it is from it. Abu Haywa and Qatada read "tuzayilu" (تُزايِلُوا) with an alif after the zay, meaning: these departed from those, and those from these. His saying ﴿from them﴾ (مِنهُمْ) is for specifying the category when the pronoun in "tazayyalu" refers to all, both believers and disbelievers. Al-Nahhas said: it has been said that His saying ﴿and had it not been for believing men﴾ up to the end of the verse means those in the loins of the disbelievers who would believe in the future of time; al-Tha'labi and al-Naqqash related this from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, from the Prophet ﷺ, as a marfu' report.

The "zealotry" (الحَمِيَّةَ) that they placed was the zealotry of the people of Makkah in barring. Al-Zuhri said: the zealotry of Suhayl and those who witnessed the conclusion of the truce was in refusing that he write "In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate," and they persisted until he wrote "In Your name, O God"; likewise they refused that he write "This is what Muhammad, the Messenger of God, agreed to," and they persisted until the Prophet ﷺ said to 'Ali, may God be pleased with him: "Erase, and write: This is what Muhammad ibn 'Abdullah agreed to..." the hadith. God made it jahiliyya zealotry because it was without proof and in other than its proper place; for if the Messenger of God ﷺ had come to them as a warrior, they would have been excused in their zealotry, but he came honouring the House, not intending war, so their zealotry was pure jahiliyya.

"Al-sakina" (السَكِينَةُ) is tranquillity in submission to the command of the Messenger of God ﷺ, trust in the promise of God, obedience, and the removal of the arrogance that afflicted 'Umar and others. As for ﴿the word of piety﴾ (كَلِمَةَ التَقْوى): the majority said: it is "There is no god but God," and this is related from the Prophet ﷺ. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: it is "There is no god but God alone, without partner, to Him is the dominion and to Him is the praise, and He is capable of all things." Abu Hurayra and 'Ata' al-Khurasani said: it is "There is no god but God, Muhammad is the Messenger of God." 'Ali ibn Abi Talib said: it is "There is no god but God, and God is greatest," related by al-Tha'labi from Ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with them both. All these sayings are close in meaning and fine, because this word protects from the Fire, so it is the word of piety. Al-Zuhri said, from al-Musawwar and Marwan: the word of piety referred to is "In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate," which the disbelievers of Quraysh refused; so God imposed it upon the believers and made them more deserving of it; and "There is no god but God" is more deserving of the name "word of piety" than "In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate." In the codex of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, is: "and they were its people and more deserving of it." The meaning: they were its people absolutely in the knowledge of God and His prior decree concerning them. It was also said: more deserving of it than the Jews and Christians in this world; and it was said: its people in the Hereafter, in reward. His saying ﴿And God is ever Knowing of all things﴾ indicates His knowledge of the believers because of whom He repelled the Quraysh disbelievers, (p-٦٨٦) and His knowledge of the aspect of benefit in the truce of al-Hudaybiyya. It is reported that when it was concluded, people were secure during that period from war and strife, and they mingled, the call of Islam rose high, and everyone among the Arabs who had understanding submitted to it; and the number of Muslims increased many times over what it had been before. This implies that the Messenger of God ﷺ, in the year of al-Hudaybiyya, was with fourteen hundred men; then he marched to Makkah two years later with ten thousand horsemen, ﷺ.

The commentary of Ibn ʿAṭiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on Surah 48, verses 27–29 (part 1 of 2):

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Allah has certainly fulfilled the vision for His Messenger in truth: you will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, secure, with your heads shaved and your hair cut short, without fear. He knew what you did not know, and He made, besides that, a near victory.﴾ ﴿It is He who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, to make it prevail over all religion, and Allah suffices as a witness.﴾ ﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and those with him are severe against the disbelievers and merciful among themselves. You see them bowing and prostrating, seeking bounty from Allah and His pleasure. Their mark is on their faces, the trace of prostration. That is their description in the Torah, and their description in the Gospel is like a seed that sends out its shoot, strengthens it, so it grows thick and stands firm on its stalk, pleasing the sowers, so that He may enrage the disbelievers by them. Allah has promised those among them who believe and do righteous deeds forgiveness and a great reward.﴾

It is narrated in the tafsir (exegesis) of this verse that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out for the ʿUmrah, he saw in his sleep that he, along with his companions, was circumambulating the House, some of them shaving their heads and some cutting their hair short. Mujāhid said: "He saw that at al-Ḥudaybiyyah." So he informed the people of this vision, and all of them were confident that it would come true on that journey. It had already been decreed in Allah's knowledge that it would happen, but not in that direction. It is also narrated that the vision of the Prophet (ﷺ) was only that an angel came to him and said to him: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, secure, with your heads shaved and your hair cut short﴾, and that by this he knew most people. When Allah decreed the treaty at al-Ḥudaybiyyah, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was distressed, and the hypocrites said: "Where is the vision?" Something of this doubt entered the hearts of the Muslims, so Allah, the Exalted, revealed: ﴿Allah has certainly fulfilled the vision for His Messenger in truth﴾. The word ﴿"ṣadaqa"﴾ here takes two objects; you say: "I told Zayd the news (ṣadaqtu Zaydan al-ḥadītha)." The lām in ﴿"latadkhulunna"﴾ is the lām of oath that the verb "ṣadaqa" requires, since it belongs to the category of "clarifying and confirming," and similar expressions that imply an oath.

The people differed about the meaning of the exception (istithnāʾ) in this verse. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿"fa-ʾāzarahu"﴾. Its pattern (wazn) is "afʿalahu," as said by al-Ḥasan. Abu 'Ali (al-Fārisī) preferred this reading. Ibn Dhakwān alone recited "fa-ʾazrahu" on the pattern "faʿlahu," without the long vowel (madd). All of this carries two meanings. The first is that it equalled it in height. From this is the line of Imru' al-Qays:

*"In a valley whose plants have grown up around the ḍāl (a thorny tree), with the passing of armies, victorious and defeated."*

That is, it is a place whose plants were not grazed, so they grew until they matched the ḍāl trees. On this meaning, the subject (fāʿil) is the shoot (shaṭʾ). The second meaning is that "ʾāzarahu" or "ʾazarahu" means he helped it and strengthened it, derived from al-izr (the waist-wrapper) and its tightening. The subject may be the shoot, and it may be the crop (zarʿ), since each of them strengthens the other. Mujāhid and others said: its pattern is "fāʿalahu." The first view is more correct, that its pattern is "afʿalahu." This is shown by the words of the poet:

*"He has no wealth except a camel-colt, which he binds with a wrap, and a thirty-year-old she-camel, and a daughter of the mountain."*

Ibn Kathīr recited "ʿalā suʾqihi" with a hamza (ʿalā suʾqihi), and this is a weak dialect, in which they hamzate a waw preceded by a damma. From this is the line of the poet:

*"Ḥabbu al-Muʾqidān is dearer to me than Mūsā."*

(p-693) The clause ﴿yuʿjibu al-zurrāʿ﴾ ("it pleases the sowers") is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). If it pleases the sowers, it is more fitting that it pleases others, because there is no flaw in it, since it has pleased those who know flaws. Had it been defective, it would not have pleased them. Here the parable is complete.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿liyaghīẓa bihimu al-kuffār﴾ ("that He may enrage the disbelievers by them"). This is the start of a speech, and before it there is an omitted clause whose sense is: Allah the Exalted made them with this description so that He may enrage the disbelievers by them. Here "al-kuffār" means the polytheists. Al-Ḥasan said: among the enraging of the disbelievers was the statement of ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, in Makkah: "No one shall worship Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in secret after today." Allah the Exalted's words ﴿minhum﴾ ("of them") are for specifying the kind (bayān al-jins), not for partitioning (tabʿīḍ), because it is a promise of hope for all of them.

The tafsir of Surah al-Fatḥ is complete, and all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 48, verses 27–29 (part 2 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿"fa-ʾāzarahu"﴾. Its pattern (wazn) is "afʿalahu," as said by al-Ḥasan. Abu 'Ali (al-Fārisī) preferred this reading. Ibn Dhakwān alone recited "fa-ʾazrahu" on the pattern "faʿlahu," without the long vowel (madd). All of this carries two meanings. The first is that it equalled it in height. From this is the line of Imru' al-Qays:

*"In a valley whose plants have grown up around the ḍāl (a thorny tree), with the passing of armies, victorious and defeated."*

That is, it is a place whose plants were not grazed, so they grew until they matched the ḍāl trees. On this meaning, the subject (fāʿil) is the shoot (shaṭʾ). The second meaning is that "ʾāzarahu" or "ʾazarahu" means he helped it and strengthened it, derived from al-izr (the waist-wrapper) and its tightening. The subject may be the shoot, and it may be the crop (zarʿ), since each of them strengthens the other. Mujāhid and others said: its pattern is "fāʿalahu." The first view is more correct, that its pattern is "afʿalahu." This is shown by the words of the poet:

*"He has no wealth except a camel-colt, which he binds with a wrap, and a thirty-year-old she-camel, and a daughter of the mountain."*

Ibn Kathīr recited "ʿalā suʾqihi" with a hamza (ʿalā suʾqihi), and this is a weak dialect, in which they hamzate a waw preceded by a damma. From this is the line of the poet:

*"Ḥabbu al-Muʾqidān is dearer to me than Mūsā."*

(p-693) The clause ﴿yuʿjibu al-zurrāʿ﴾ ("it pleases the sowers") is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). If it pleases the sowers, it is more fitting that it pleases others, because there is no flaw in it, since it has pleased those who know flaws. Had it been defective, it would not have pleased them. Here the parable is complete.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿liyaghīẓa bihimu al-kuffār﴾ ("that He may enrage the disbelievers by them"). This is the start of a speech, and before it there is an omitted clause whose sense is: Allah the Exalted made them with this description so that He may enrage the disbelievers by them. Here "al-kuffār" means the polytheists. Al-Ḥasan said: among the enraging of the disbelievers was the statement of ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, in Makkah: "No one shall worship Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in secret after today." Allah the Exalted's words ﴿minhum﴾ ("of them") are for specifying the kind (bayān al-jins), not for partitioning (tabʿīḍ), because it is a promise of hope for all of them.

The tafsir of Surah al-Fatḥ is complete, and all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

The commentary of Ibn ʿAṭiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on Surah 48, verses 27–29 (part 1 of 2):

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Allah has certainly fulfilled the vision for His Messenger in truth: you will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, secure, with your heads shaved and your hair cut short, without fear. He knew what you did not know, and He made, besides that, a near victory.﴾ ﴿It is He who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, to make it prevail over all religion, and Allah suffices as a witness.﴾ ﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and those with him are severe against the disbelievers and merciful among themselves. You see them bowing and prostrating, seeking bounty from Allah and His pleasure. Their mark is on their faces, the trace of prostration. That is their description in the Torah, and their description in the Gospel is like a seed that sends out its shoot, strengthens it, so it grows thick and stands firm on its stalk, pleasing the sowers, so that He may enrage the disbelievers by them. Allah has promised those among them who believe and do righteous deeds forgiveness and a great reward.﴾

It is narrated in the tafsir (exegesis) of this verse that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out for the ʿUmrah, he saw in his sleep that he, along with his companions, was circumambulating the House, some of them shaving their heads and some cutting their hair short. Mujāhid said: "He saw that at al-Ḥudaybiyyah." So he informed the people of this vision, and all of them were confident that it would come true on that journey. It had already been decreed in Allah's knowledge that it would happen, but not in that direction. It is also narrated that the vision of the Prophet (ﷺ) was only that an angel came to him and said to him: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, secure, with your heads shaved and your hair cut short﴾, and that by this he knew most people. When Allah decreed the treaty at al-Ḥudaybiyyah, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was distressed, and the hypocrites said: "Where is the vision?" Something of this doubt entered the hearts of the Muslims, so Allah, the Exalted, revealed: ﴿Allah has certainly fulfilled the vision for His Messenger in truth﴾. The word ﴿"ṣadaqa"﴾ here takes two objects; you say: "I told Zayd the news (ṣadaqtu Zaydan al-ḥadītha)." The lām in ﴿"latadkhulunna"﴾ is the lām of oath that the verb "ṣadaqa" requires, since it belongs to the category of "clarifying and confirming," and similar expressions that imply an oath.

The people differed about the meaning of the exception (istithnāʾ) in this verse. Some interpreters said: it is an exception from the angel who informed the Prophet (ﷺ), in his statement, so Allah related his words as they occurred. Others said: it is a teaching from Allah to His servants in His etiquette in using the exception with every act that is bound to happen, whether it is something that must certainly occur or something that may or may not occur. Some scholars said: He made the exception from the perspective of each individual person, since whenever a person applies this promise to himself, it is possible that it may be fulfilled or not fulfilled, for a person may die, fall ill, or be absent, and each one in himself needs the exception. Therefore, the Mighty and Majestic made the exception in general, since among them there would certainly be some who die. Others said: He made the exception because of His words, the Exalted: ﴿"āminīn"﴾ (secure), not because of His informing about entering. So the exception is, as it were, placed after its proper position.

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is no difference between making the exception because of the security or because of the entering, for Allah, blessed and exalted, has informed of both, and confidence was placed in both matters. So whichever of the two the exception is from, it is an exception from something obligatory.

Some people said: "in" (in) means "idh" (when), so it is as if He, the Exalted, said: "When Allah wills." This is good in its meaning, but the use of "in" to mean "idh" is not found in the language of the Arabs. There are still other confused opinions about this exception, beyond these, which have no benefit in them; I have abridged them. Ibn Masʿūd recited: "in shāʾa Allāhu lā takhāfūna" in place of "āminīn."

When this verse was revealed, the Muslims knew that the vision referred to what they would experience in the time to come, and their hearts were reassured and calmed by that. So in the following year they went out. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out for Makkah in Dhū al-Qaʿdah in the year seven, and he and his companions entered it for three days, and his vision came true. His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿He knew what you did not know﴾ means what He had decreed of the manifestation of Islam during that period and the entry of people into it, and also the believers who were in Makkah, through whom Allah repelled harm. His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿besides that﴾ means: before that, and in what is near to you.

The people differed about the "near victory." Many of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, said: it is the Pledge of Riḍwān (Bayʿat al-Riḍwān). It is narrated from Mujāhid and Ibn Isḥāq that it is the treaty at al-Ḥudaybiyyah. It has been narrated that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him, said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Is it a victory, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Yes." Ibn Zayd said: the near victory is the conquest of Makkah. This is weak, because the conquest of Makkah did not occur besides the entry of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions into Makkah; rather it came a year after that, for the conquest took place in the year eight of the Hijrah. It is fitting that "the victory" here be a generic noun that encompasses everything in which there was manifest victory and opening for the Prophet (ﷺ). Makkī has related, in the chronological arrangement of the years of these reports, an erroneous statement from Quṭrub, in which he made the conquest in the year ten and placed the pilgrimage of Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, before the conquest. All of that is confusion and speculation about matters that he did not master with knowledge.

Some people considered that the word ﴿"liyuẓhirahu"﴾ (to make it prevail) requires that it erase others by it. Therefore they said: this report will become manifest in existence at the descent of ʿĪsā ibn Maryam, peace be upon them both, for at that time no religion will remain except Islam. This is the view of al-Ṭabarī and al-Thaʿlabī. Others held that "ẓuhūr" (prevailing) means elevation, even if some parts of the other religion remain, and this is present now in the religion of Islam, for it has covered most of the earth and prevailed over every religion. His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿and Allah suffices as a witness﴾ means: as a witness. This has two possible meanings: first, a witness to you of this report and one who informs you of it; second, a witness against those disbelievers who deny the affair of Muḥammad (ﷺ) and who harbor rejection in their hearts, and one who punishes them by the judgment of testimony. So the verse, according to this, is a warning to the disbelievers who were stubborn about writing "Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." Allah, blessed and exalted, responded to them with this entire verse.

Some interpreters said: "Muḥammad" is the subject, "Rasūl Allāh" is an attribute of it, "alladhīna" is conjoined to it, ﴿"ashiddāʾu"﴾ is a predicate about all of them, and "ruḥamāʾu" is a predicate after a predicate. Abū al-Fatḥ said: if you wish, you may put "ashiddāʾa" in the accusative as praise.

Mālik ibn Anas said: their foreheads were dusty from much prostration on the ground, and the trace of that remained upon them when they wiped them. ʿIkrimah also said this. Abū al-ʿĀliyah said: they prostrated on the earth, not on garments. Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, Khālid al-Ḥanafī, and ʿAṭiyyah said: it is a promise of their state on the Day of Resurrection, that Allah, blessed and exalted, will make for them a light from the trace of prostration.

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Just as He makes a blaze (ghurrah) from the trace of ablution... the ḥadīth. This interpretation is supported by the connection of the statement with His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿grace from Allah and His pleasure﴾, as if He, the Exalted, said: their mark, in attaining His pleasure on the Day of Resurrection, is their mark on their faces from the trace of prostration.
